subject: Agriculture
title: Soil-Borne Pathogens
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Soil-Borne Pathogens.

hook.text: Fusarium wilt killed billions of Gros Michel bananas in the 1950s. Now Panama Disease TR4 threatens the Cavendish.

buildup.text: Soil-borne fungi persist for decades. Once a field is infested, it stays contaminated indefinitely.

discovery.text: Fusarium enters through roots and clogs the plant's water-conducting vessels. The banana wilts from within.

twist.text: There is no fungicide that works against TR4 in the field. Resistant varieties are the only long-term answer.

climax.text: The world's banana supply depends on one genetically identical variety. If TR4 spreads, there's no backup.

punchline.text: One clone. One disease. A global fruit at risk.

quiz.question: Why is the global banana supply vulnerable to Panama Disease TR4?
options: All commercial Cavendish bananas are genetically identical clones

details.summary: Soil-borne pathogens are fungi, bacteria, and nematodes that live in the soil and attack plant roots, causing wilting, root rot, and damping-off. This topic covers major soil-borne diseases, how they persist for years underground, and the challenges of managing them.
details.whyItMatters: Soil-borne pathogens are among the hardest agricultural diseases to manage because they survive for years in soil and cannot be reached by most surface-applied treatments.
takeaways: Soil-borne pathogens include Fusarium, Pythium, Rhizoctonia, and Verticillium fungi
They can persist in soil for years as resistant spores even without a host crop
Management relies on crop rotation, soil health, resistant varieties, and biofumigation

faq.question: Why are soil-borne pathogens so difficult to control?
faq.answer: Soil-borne pathogens produce resting structures (spores, sclerotia) that survive in soil for 5-20 years without a host. They are protected from surface-applied chemicals by soil particles. Once established in a field, complete eradication is nearly impossible.

faq.question: What strategies help manage soil-borne crop diseases?
faq.answer: Long crop rotations (4-7 years) reduce pathogen buildup. Cover crops like mustard release natural biofumigants. Healthy soil biology with diverse microbes suppresses pathogens through competition. Resistant varieties and soil solarization also provide control in appropriate climates.
